introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá taught a great deal through stories: tales from Rumi and the lore of Islam, sayings attributed to Jesus that the Gospels do not contain, incidents from his own travels and from the prisons and journeys of Bahá’u’lláh, jokes, and dreams. This guide gathers a hundred of them, with a few from Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb. Beside each is set a passage from elsewhere: often the scriptural story being retold or alluded to, in the words of the King James Bible or Pickthall's Qur’an; sometimes a proverb that carries the same point; and now and then a voice, from Aristotle and the Talmud to Shakespeare, Milton and Shelley, that tells the tale another way or asks what stories are for.
questions: One talk says that some stories have no historical foundation and still carry a deep lesson. Aristotle said poetry is more philosophical than history. What makes a story true?
Compare the Pharisee and the publican, or the coin for Caesar, as told here and as the Gospel tells it. What changes in the retelling?
Several stories are funny. What can a joke do in teaching that an argument cannot?
"Difficulty and ease are mostly in the mind." Milton gave almost the same words to Satan. When does the saying help, and when might it mislead?
The accounts of illness stopping at the gates of ‘Akká stand here beside the warning of Jesus about the tower in Siloam. How should stories of protection be told?
The last stretch is about dreams. How do Jeremiah and the Preacher suggest that a dream be weighed?

outside.why: The letter to the Hebrews recalls Abraham's hospitality: some have entertained angels without knowing it.
Jesus gives the reason the story gives: God sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust alike.
Paul asks his readers to fix their minds on whatever is lovely and of good report.
Jesus asks why we see the speck in a brother's eye and miss the beam in our own.
This is the parable as Luke tells it, with its closing rule about the humble and the exalted.
The Talmud tells the same story of an old man planting a carob tree: as my ancestors planted for me, I plant for those who come after.
Proverbs observes that company shapes a person: walk with the wise and become wise.
The first letter of John asks for love in deed and in truth, and not in word only.
Aristotle held that poetry is more philosophical than history, because it tells what may happen and not only what did. Does a story need to have happened in order to teach?
Proverbs says it is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly.
In the parable of Jesus the master's praise for a servant is that he was good and faithful.
Proverbs prefers a dinner of herbs where love is to a fattened ox with hatred.
Jesus weighs gifts in the same way: the poor widow's two small coins were more than the offerings of the rich.
Paul asks believers to weep with those who weep, as the dwellers of the pavilion do here.
The Qur’an says that piety is not reached until one gives of what one loves.
This is the verse said to have been revealed on the occasion the story relates.
Job gives Ayaz's answer: shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?
Paul says that he has learned to be content in whatever state he is, full or hungry.
Jesus warns against doing good in order to be seen and praised by others.
The letter of James says that to wish the hungry well without feeding them is a dead faith.
Peter asks how often he must forgive, and is told seventy times seven.
Paul asks that each bear the burdens of the other, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Peter also declared that he would die with his master, a few hours before he denied him.
Proverbs says that a merry heart does good like a medicine, which is how the quince was prescribed.
The letter of James warns against being hearers of the word only and not doers.
The Preacher allows a time to laugh among the times of a life.
Jesus tells his followers not to pile up words in prayer as though they would be heard for saying much.
Isaiah speaks of worship offered with the lips while the heart is somewhere else.
A psalm makes the same appeal to experience over description: taste and see.
A psalm exclaims how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity.
Jesus tells of a rich man who stored up goods for many years and died that night.
Jesus compares religious show to whitewashed tombs, fair outside and foul within.
Shakespeare's Richard explains how he seems a saint when most he plays the devil.
Hamlet notes with amazement that one may smile, and smile, and be a villain.
Solomon settled a case with two equal claims by a test that showed who really cared for the child.
Amos asks that justice roll down like waters, whoever stands in its way.
Isaiah describes a judge who decides with righteousness for the poor and the meek.
Jesus says that where a person's treasure is, the heart will be also. What would you endure a beating for sooner than give up?
Paul's charge to the Corinthians is the veterans' charge to their officers: stand fast and be strong.
This is the saying of Jesus behind the story: foxes have holes and birds have nests, but he has nowhere to lay his head.
This is the Preacher's own account of trying every pleasure and finding it vanity.
A psalm gives the cry of such a seeker: my soul thirsts for God, for the living God.
Micah asks the same question at the same threshold: with what shall I come before the Lord?
The voice from the whirlwind asks Job where he was when the earth was founded. Who is in a position to set the test?
Jesus gave the same answer on the pinnacle of the temple: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
Paul speaks of beholding glory as in a mirror and being changed into what is reflected.
The Qur’an gives the same instruction: travel in the land and see the end of those who went before.
Shelley's traveller finds a boast carved on a ruined statue in an empty desert. What does a ruin teach that a sermon cannot?
Genesis begins the story of Abraham with a command to leave his country, and a promise.
The letter to the Hebrews says of the patriarchs that they lived as strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Paul traces the same schooling: tribulation produces patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
Nehemiah's builders prayed and also kept a watch. What does this story say about precautions and where safety comes from?
Paul asks that evil be overcome with good and that vengeance be left alone.
Milton gives almost the same sentence to Satan, consoling himself in hell: the mind can make a heaven of hell. When is "difficulty is in the mind" wisdom, and when is it a way of avoiding the facts?
Hamlet says that nothing is good or bad but thinking makes it so.
Epictetus taught that people are disturbed not by things but by the views they take of them.
Proverbs advises letting another praise you, a stranger, and not your own mouth or lips.
Proverbs warns that flattery spreads a net for the feet of the one who is flattered.
Jesus counts a visit to the sick as a visit to himself.
Paul wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female, a sentence long in finding its fulfilment.
Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like the headland against which the waves break and which stands unmoved.
A psalm promises that the pestilence that walks in darkness will not come near the one who trusts.
Jesus asked whether those on whom a tower fell were worse than their neighbours, and said no. How should stories of protection be told beside that warning?
Paul quotes the prophet's joy over those who carry good news to a place that has not heard it.
Paul was told that grace was enough for him, since strength is made perfect in weakness.
The disciples at Emmaus remembered an evening by how their hearts had burned.
Stephen, the first to die for his message, died praying for those who killed him.
Paul counted everything as loss for the sake of the one he had found.
Matthew says that Jesus did not speak to the crowds without a story.
This is the challenge Mordecai put to Esther: who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
This is Luke's account of the supper to which the talk refers.
Paul in Athens began from what his hearers already honoured and named the one they did not know.
On Carmel Elijah put his question to the people: how long will you waver between two opinions?
Zechariah heard that it is not by might nor by power, but by the Spirit.
This is the verse about Noah's son to which the letter refers.
Jesus says that his brother and sister and mother are those who do the will of his Father.
Jesus calls blessed those who are persecuted for his sake, as the first callers to prayer were.
Amos says of himself that he was no prophet but a herdsman when he was called.
Jesus calls blessed those who have not seen and yet have believed.
Peter writes to people who love one they have never seen, and rejoice in him all the same.
The neighbours of Jesus knew him as the carpenter's son, a trade this letter honours through Noah.
Isaiah cried out that he was a man of unclean lips, and his mouth was touched with a coal from the altar.
This is the Gospel account of the coin and the answer about Caesar and God.
Jesus has the same image for the scruples of the unjust: they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.
Luke records that Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer.
This is the verse of the Qur’an revealed in answer to that taunt.
This is the account in Luke of the moment after the third denial, when Peter remembered and wept.
This is the verse the robber is said to have overheard, asking whether the time has not come for hearts to submit.
Augustine's life was turned in the same way, by a voice overheard from a neighbouring house.
Jesus tells of a merchant who sold all that he had to buy one pearl.
The book of Job says that God speaks in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls.
Jeremiah says: let the prophet who has a dream tell a dream; what is chaff to wheat? How is a claimed dream to be weighed?
Isaiah says that as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are God's ways higher than ours.
The Preacher finds vanity in the multitude of dreams. What separates a dream worth recounting from one that is only sleep talking?
Genesis tells of Joseph's dreams and of how his brothers took them.
Joel foretells a day when the old shall dream dreams and the young see visions.
The letter of James holds up the patience of Job and the end the Lord gave him.
These are the first words of Job after his losses: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.
Job uses the same image of himself: when he has tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
Seneca has the proverb in a line: fire tries gold, and misfortune tries the brave.

luke-pharisee-and-publican.text: Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted

philippians-think-on-these-things.text: Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things

proverbs-bear-robbed-of-her-whelps.text: Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly

matthew-though-i-should-die-with-thee.text: Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples

kings-judgment-of-solomon.text: And the king said, Bring me a sword. And they brought a sword before the king. And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other. Then spake the woman whose the living child was unto the king, for her bowels yearned upon her son, and she said, O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it. But the other said, Let it be neither mine nor thine, but divide it. Then the king answered and said, Give her the living child, and in no wise slay it: she is the mother thereof

micah-wherewith-shall-i-come.text: Wherewith shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul

matthew-sick-and-ye-visited-me.text: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me

psalm-pestilence-that-walketh.text: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day; Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday. A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee

esther-for-such-a-time.text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this

luke-this-do-in-remembrance.text: And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me

peter-having-not-seen-ye-love.text: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory

james-pray-one-for-another.text: Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much

isaiah-unclean-lips.text: Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts. Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged

job-in-a-dream.text: For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed; Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction

ecclesiastes-multitude-of-dreams.text: For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God

jeremiah-chaff-to-the-wheat.text: The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the Lord

matthew-without-a-parable.text: All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world

genesis-josephs-dream.text: And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it his brethren: and they hated him yet the more. And he said unto them, Hear, I pray you, this dream which I have dreamed: For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf. And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words

luke-all-night-in-prayer.text: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God

quran-travel-in-the-land.text: Say (O Muhammad, to the disbelievers): Travel in the land, and see the nature of the consequence for those who were before you! Most of them were idolaters.

quran-without-posterity.text: Lo! it is thy insulter (and not thou) who is without posterity.

shakespeare-thinking-makes-it-so.text: there is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so
shakespeare-thinking-makes-it-so.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

epictetus-not-by-things.text: Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things
epictetus-not-by-things.author: Epictetus

aristotle-poetry-more-philosophical.text: The true difference is that one relates what has happened, the other what may happen. Poetry, therefore, is a more philosophical and a higher thing than history: for poetry tends to express the universal, history the particular
aristotle-poetry-more-philosophical.author: Aristotle

talmud-world-full-of-carob-trees.text: That man himself found a world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I too am planting for my descendants

proverbs-let-another-praise-thee.text: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips

proverbs-flattereth-his-neighbour.text: A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet
